claim: Maize Rtn1 and Rtn2 control ER homeostasis and autophagic flux in endosperm aleurone cells.
source: We have found that maize Rtn1 and Rtn2 control ER homeostasis and autophagic flux in endosperm aleurone cells, where the ER accumulates lipid droplets and synthesizes storage protein accretions metabolized during germination.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, including electron microscopy, immunoblot analysis, and fluorescence microscopy showing altered autophagy and ER stress in rtn mutants.

claim: Maize Rtn1 and Rtn2 are expressed in the endosperm.
source: Maize Rtn1 and Rtn2 are expressed in the endosperm, localize to the ER, and re-model ER architecture in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: Expression data from RNA-sequencing databases and RT-PCR experiments confirm expression in endosperm tissues.

claim: Maize Rtn1 and Rtn2 localize to the ER.
source: Maize Rtn1 and Rtn2 are expressed in the endosperm, localize to the ER, and re-model ER architecture in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: Colocalization with ER marker mCherry-KDEL in protoplasts demonstrates ER localization (Figure 1C).

claim: Maize Rtn1 and Rtn2 re-model ER architecture in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Maize Rtn1 and Rtn2 are expressed in the endosperm, localize to the ER, and re-model ER architecture in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: Increasing expression of Rtn2-mCherry leads to architectural reorganization of the ER as shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Rtn1 and Rtn2 interact with Atg8a using four Atg8-interacting motifs (AIMs).
source: Rtn1 and Rtn2 interact with Atg8a using four Atg8-interacting motifs (AIMs) located at the C-terminus, cytoplasmic loop, and within the transmembrane segments.
evidence: Y2H assays and co-immunoprecipitation experiments with AIM mutants demonstrate that four AIMs are required for Atg8a binding (Figure 2).

claim: The four AIMs in Rtn1 and Rtn2 are located at the C-terminus, cytoplasmic loop, and within the transmembrane segments.
source: Rtn1 and Rtn2 interact with Atg8a using four Atg8-interacting motifs (AIMs) located at the C-terminus, cytoplasmic loop, and within the transmembrane segments.
evidence: Sequence analysis and mutagenesis experiments identify AIMs at these specific locations (Figure 2C).

claim: Binding between Rtn2 and Atg8 is elevated upon ER stress.
source: Binding between Rtn2 and Atg8 is elevated upon ER stress.
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation assays show approximately 3-fold increase in binding between GFP-Atg8a and HA-Rtn2 upon DTT treatment (Figure 4B-D).

claim: Maize rtn2 mutants display increased autophagy.
source: Maize rtn2 mutants display increased autophagy and up-regulation of an ER stress-responsive chaperone.
evidence: Electron microscopy shows increased cytoplasmic contents in vacuoles (Figure 5), and YFP-Atg8a flux assays show elevated autophagic flux in rtn2 mutants (Figure 6).

claim: Maize rtn2 mutants display up-regulation of an ER stress-responsive chaperone.
source: Maize rtn2 mutants display increased autophagy and up-regulation of an ER stress-responsive chaperone.
evidence: qRT-PCR shows approximately 2-fold increase in Bip2 transcript levels in rtn2-2 aleurone samples (Figure 7B).

claim: Maize Rtn1 and Rtn2 act as receptors for autophagy-mediated ER turnover.
source: We propose that maize Rtn1 and Rtn2 act as receptors for autophagy-mediated ER turnover, and thus are critical for ER homeostasis and suppression of ER stress.
evidence: Multiple lines of evidence including Atg8 binding, sequestration into autophagosomes during ER stress, and phenotypes of rtn mutants support this conclusion.

claim: Maize Rtn1 and Rtn2 are critical for ER homeostasis and suppression of ER stress.
source: We propose that maize Rtn1 and Rtn2 act as receptors for autophagy-mediated ER turnover, and thus are critical for ER homeostasis and suppression of ER stress.
evidence: rtn2 mutants show elevated ER stress markers and increased autophagy, indicating their role in maintaining ER homeostasis (Figure 7).

claim: Alanine substitutions in four AIMs (AIM1, AIM2, AIM5, and AIM6) abolished Atg8a binding.

claim: Rtn2 does not redistribute within the ER in response to protein folding stress.
source: We also tested whether Rtn2 redistributes within the ER in response to ER stress by examining the localization of Rtn2-mCherry and CFP-KDEL in protoplasts incubated for 3 hr with or without DTT. We did not detect changes in the mCherry signal relative to that of CFP after DTT treatment (Figure 4A), suggesting that Rtn2 does not redistribute within the ER in response to protein folding stress.
evidence: Colocalization analysis shows no change in Pearson correlation coefficients after DTT treatment (Figure 4A).

claim: An approximately 3-fold increase in binding between GFP-Atg8a and HA-Rtn2 was seen upon DTT treatment.
source: To assay whether the affinity of Rtn2 for Atg8a was enhanced under ER-stress, we incubated protoplasts expressing GFP-Atg8a and HA-Rtn2 for 3 hr in the presence or absence of 2 mM DTT, and then co-immunoprecipitated GFP-Atg8a with anti-HA antibodies. An approximately 3-fold increase in the binding between GFP-Atg8a and HA-Rtn2 was seen upon DTT treatment (Figure 4B–D; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation and densitometric quantification show increased binding (Figure 4B-D).

claim: Exposing Arabidopsis protoplasts to 5 μg/mL tunicamycin for 3 hr led to increased binding between GFP-Atg8a and HA-Rtn2.

Similar to DTT, exposing Arabidopsis protoplasts to 5 μg/mL tunicamycin for 3 hr led to increased binding between GFP-Atg8a and HA-Rtn2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation assays show increased binding after tunicamycin treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D,E).

claim: AIM1 within the C-terminal tail of Rtn2 is required for the increased binding of Rtn2 to Atg8a upon DTT exposure.
source: To identify which AIMs in Rtn2 might be responsible for the enhanced binding to Atg8a under ER stress, we performed co-immunoprecipitation assays with GFP-ATG8a and HA-tagged versions of either Rtn2, Rtn2(mAIM1), or Rtn2(mAIM1,2,5,6) expressed in protoplasts treated with or without DTT. As shown in Figure 4B and C, no increase in Atg8a binding was seen for the Rtn2(mAIM1) protein, indicating that AIM1 within the C-terminal tail of Rtn2 was required for the increased binding of Rtn2 to Atg8a upon DTT exposure (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation with AIM mutants shows AIM1 is required for enhanced binding (Figure 4B,C).

evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation shows no binding for quadruple AIM mutant.

claim: GFP-Atg8a(mLDS) did not interact with HA-Rtn2 in protoplasts incubated with or without DTT.

evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation with LDS mutant shows no interaction (Figure 4D).

claim: The elevated accumulation of cytoplasmic material inside aleurone vacuoles was no longer evident in rtn2-2 atg12-2 plants.

The elevated accumulation of cytoplasmic material inside aleurone vacuoles was no longer evident in rtn2-2 atg12-2 plants (Figure 5H–J), indicating that the loss of Rtn2 leads to an increase in Atg8-mediated macro-autophagy.

claim: YFP-Atg8a signal in wild-type aleurone cells localized to both the cytosol and cytoplasmic puncta of less than 1 μm in diameter.
source: To confirm the mis-regulation of autophagy in rtn1/2 aleurone cells seen by transmission electron microscopy, we introgressed the rtn2-3 mutation into maize wild type (W22) and atg12 mutant plants expressing the YFP-Atg8a reporter, which labels autophagosomes upon lipidation and is delivered to the vacuole as part of the autophagic body (Li et al., 2015). As expected, the YFP-Atg8a signal in wild-type aleurone cells localized to both the cytosol and cytoplasmic puncta of less than 1 μm in diameter, which likely represented autophagosomes (Figure 6A,B; red arrowheads), but remained exclusively cytosolic when either the atg12-1 or atg12-2 (Li et al., 2015) mutations are introduced (Figure 6C,D,H,I).
evidence: Confocal microscopy shows YFP-Atg8a localization pattern (Figure 6A,B).

claim: The relative abundance of free YFP was higher in rtn2-3 aleurone samples compared to wild type.
source: We next analyzed autophagic flux in aleurone and starchy endosperm cells by measuring the release of YFP from the YFP-Atg8a reporter. When proteins with GFP-based fluorescent tags are delivered to vacuoles, the GFP/YFP moiety is quickly released by vacuolar proteases and stably accumulates in the vacuolar lumen, which can then be assayed by immunoblot analysis of total cell lysates with anti-GFP antibodies (Li et al., 2015). Thus, the ratio of free YFP to YFP-Atg8a informs on the extent of vacuolar YFP-Atg8 delivery and can be used as a proxy for measuring overall autophagic flux. As shown in Figure 6J and K, the relative abundance of free YFP was higher in the rtn2-3 aleurone samples compared to those from wild type, but was similar in the two starchy endosperm samples (Figure 6J,K), indicating that autophagic flux was specifically elevated in aleurone cells of the rtn2-3 mutant.
evidence: Immunoblot analysis and quantification show increased YFP/YFP-Atg8a ratio in rtn2-3 aleurone (Figure 6J,K).
